artworks.title: Herakles and the Lernaean Hydra (Caeretan black-figure hydria)
artworks.description: On this archaic Caeretan black-figure water-jar (hydria), the hero Herakles strides against the Lernaean Hydra, whose many serpentine necks fan out from a single coiled body in a writhing tangle. The painter gives the monster the multiplying heads of the myth, and beside Herakles his nephew Iolaos assists with the torch used to cauterize the severed stumps so they cannot regrow. Produced in Etruria around the late sixth century BC, the vase is among the earliest and most vivid surviving images of the Second Labour. It is held by the J. Paul Getty Museum (Getty Villa, inv. 83.AE.346).

artworks.title: Hercules and the Hydra
artworks.description: This small but intensely energetic Florentine panel by Antonio del Pollaiuolo shows a nude, muscular Hercules swinging his club against the Lernaean Hydra, whose multiple snake-necks rear up and lunge at him from the marshy ground. Painted for the Medici around 1475, the work is celebrated for its anatomical dynamism and its rendering of violent motion, a hallmark of Pollaiuolo's fascination with the body in action. It hangs in the Uffizi Gallery, Florence, and is paired in conception with his companion image of Hercules and Antaeus.

artworks.title: Hercules and the Lernaean Hydra
artworks.description: Gustave Moreau's grand Symbolist canvas transforms the Second Labour into a hushed, ominous tableau: a calm, statuesque Hercules confronts the towering Hydra, whose serpent heads rise on long pale necks above a foreground strewn with the corpses of the monster's victims. Moreau drew on early Greek vase imagery for the multi-headed serpent while charging the scene with brooding atmosphere and decorative detail, making the encounter a meditation on heroism against monstrous evil. The painting is held by the Art Institute of Chicago.

artworks.title: The Labours of Hercules: slaying the Lernaean Hydra (Roman mosaic)
artworks.description: A panel from a Roman floor mosaic depicting the Twelve Labours of Hercules, this section shows the hero combating the Lernaean Hydra, the water-serpent rendered with multiple coiling heads emerging from the Lernaean swamp. Such labour cycles were a popular decorative program in Roman villas, presenting Hercules as a model of virtue triumphing over chaos. The mosaic, from Roman Hispania (Liria, Valencia), is preserved in the Museo Arqueológico Nacional in Madrid.
